Part 4. The drawing model: a tutorial

4.0 The whole model on one page

Everything Sketchpad draws comes from four verbs:

  • Make a path from a rule: a line, a circle, a rose.
  • Shape it: space its points evenly, trim it, reverse it, turn it. Shaping can be repeated as often as you like.
  • Connect one or more paths into stitch lines.
  • Find the points worth naming: an end, a corner, the tip of a lobe.

Named points go into the document's point table. That is where nails come from, and where one layer's handles can be tied to another's.

[[FIG model_onepage | The drawing model: make, shape, connect, find]]
Vocabulary for this part. A path is a numbered list of points. A maker builds one; a shaper turns one path into another; a connector turns paths into stitch lines; a finder names points on a path. The point table is the document's list of numbered points. A generator is one file that strings these together into an object such as the Parabola.

Lesson 1. A path is a list of points

Under every line Sketchpad draws there is an ordered list of points. A path is that list plus one fact: whether the last point joins back to the first. In Figure 11 the line is an open path of 9 points, numbered 0 to 8. The circle is a closed path of 12, numbered 0 to 11, and on a closed path counting past 11 comes round to 0 again. That wrap-around is what makes stars and roses possible (Lesson 5).

[[FIG path_figure | An open path and a closed path]]

What to notice. The numbers are positions in the list, not names. Point 3 is "the fourth one along", whatever its coordinates are. Every rule in this tutorial is a rule about those positions.

Lesson 2. Connecting two paths: the parabola

Take two lines that meet at a corner, each divided into 8 steps, so each is a path of 9 points. The connector pairwise joins point i of the first to point i of the second, for every i (Figure 12).

[[FIG pairwise_indexed | pairwise: point i joins point i]]

Every stitch is straight. The curve is what the eye sees where the stitches crowd together: the envelope of the lines. It is a true parabola. That's why string art can make curves from straight thread, and it is the whole of what the Parabola object does.

What to notice. The arms run in a particular direction: arm 1 from its far end towards the corner, arm 2 from the corner outward. Point 0 of arm 1 is the far end; point 0 of arm 2 is the corner. Lesson 3 shows why that matters.

Lesson 3. Direction and length matter

Leave the connector alone and change only the paths (Figure 13). Reverse arm 2, so it runs from its far end back to the corner, and every stitch becomes parallel to the others: no curve at all. Make one arm shorter than the other and the curve leans. The connector never changed; only the lists it was given did.

[[FIG reverse_compare | Same connector, paths changed]]

Try it (on the kernel bench, checkpoint CP-1). Predict what pairwise(reverse(arm1), arm2) looks like before you draw it. It is the same as reversing arm 2, mirrored: parallel lines again.

Lesson 4. The same connector on other paths

Nothing in pairwise knows about lines. Give it an arc and a line and you get a curve swept between them. Give it two circles and you get a band. Start the small circle's numbering 9 places along (startAt, a shaper) and the band twists (Figure 14). This is the family Linked Circles belongs to: several circles, joined pairwise in a ring or all to all.

[[FIG same_connector_other_paths | pairwise between an arc and a line, and between two circles with a twist]]

Lesson 5. One closed path, joined to itself

A connector can join a path to itself. Three rules cover most of the classic string-art figures.

Skip. Join each point to the point s places further on (Figure 15). On a circle of 20 points with s = 7, point 0 joins 7, point 1 joins 8, and point 13 joins 20, which is past the end, so it wraps round to 0. The wrap-around is what closes the star. Chords in Ellipse is this rule on an ellipse.

[[FIG skip_examples | skip: each point joins the point s places on]]

Multiply. Join point i to point k×i (Figure 16). With k = 2 on 96 points, point 1 joins 2, point 2 joins 4, and point 50 joins 100, which wraps round to 4. The result is a cardioid, which is what the Cycloid object draws. k = 3 gives a nephroid (two lobes), k = 5 four lobes. The number of lobes is always k − 1.

[[FIG multiply_examples | multiply: point i joins point k times i]]

All pairs. Join every point to every other point (Figure 17). That is the mystic rose. The number of lines grows quickly: n points give n(n − 1)/2 lines, so 14 points give 91 lines and 30 give 435. On a board that is 435 lengths of thread, which is worth knowing before choosing n.

[[FIG allpairs_counts | allPairs: every point to every other]]

Lesson 6. Shapers: changing a path before it is connected

A shaper takes a path and returns another. Your createNodes already did several of these, fused together and for ellipses only. Version 2 takes them apart so each works on any path, in any order (Figure 18).

[[FIG shapers_figure | Shapers]]
ShaperWhat it doesTypical use
evenSpacing(path, n)Re-places n points at equal distances along the pathNails at even spacing on any curve
bias(path, b)Crowds points towards one endDenser stitching where the eye looks
jitter(path, size, seed)Moves each point a little, at random but repeatablyA hand-made look; the same seed gives the same picture
trim(path, a, b)Drops a points from the start and b from the endToday's Trim and Shorten sliders
reverse(path)Runs the list backwardsLesson 3
startAt(path, i)Renumbers a closed path to start at point iTwists (Lesson 4); turns a star without moving it
everyKth(path, k)Keeps every k-th pointFewer nails on the same curve
move, rotate, scaleMoves the pointsPlacing a path; a layer's own move and turn

What to notice. Jitter takes a seed. With the same settings and the same seed, the same picture comes back every time, which matters for a design you mean to print.

Lesson 7. Where paths come from: makers, and why parametric is not special

A maker is a rule that says where the point is at each moment t, as t runs from start to finish. Sampled at n moments, it gives a path. A line is the simplest rule: start at a and move steadily towards b. A circle goes round its centre. A Lissajous figure or a rose is just a longer formula (Figure 19). Seen this way, a "parametric drawing" is an ordinary path from an unusual maker, and everything in Lessons 2 to 6 applies to it.

[[FIG makers_figure | Three makers, one kind of result]]

One difference is real. Taking equal steps in t does not give equal spacing along a curve. On a rose, equal steps crowd the points near the centre (left of Figure 18). Nails want equal spacing, so a curve is usually followed by evenSpacing. Version 2 also keeps two samplings of a curve (Figure 20): a fine one, with many points, for drawing it smoothly on screen, and a coarse one, with one point per nail, for stitching and printing.

[[FIG two_samplings | The same curve, sampled for display and for nails]]

Lesson 8. Finding points worth naming

A finder looks at a path and names points on it (Figure 21): its ends and middle, its extremes, the tips of a rose's lobes, its cusps, the places where two paths cross. These are Phase 8b's "magic points", and they are what other layers attach to.

[[FIG finders_figure | Finders name points by what they are]]

What to notice. A finder names a point by what it is ("tip of lobe 2"), not by its position in the list ("point 17"). Change the rose from 30 points to 40 and point 17 is somewhere else, but tip 2 is still tip 2. That is what keeps attachments stable when you change a step count.

Lesson 9. Layers that use other layers

So far each drawing has made its own paths. In a figure, a layer can use paths that belong to other layers. In Figure 22, layer L3 owns no shape: it connects layer L1's circle to layer L2's line with pairwise. Move L1 or L2 and L3 follows, because it is recomputed from them.

[[FIG cross_layer | A layer that connects two other layers' paths]]

The same idea joins handles. Every handle names a numbered point in the document's point table, and a table entry is one of two kinds.

A free point holds its own position. Two handles that name the same free point are welded: there is one point and two names for it (Figure 23). Drag it and both layers redraw. There is nothing to copy and nothing to keep in step. This is your rule from October: a weld is a shared point number.

[[FIG weld_shared | Two layers name point 11]]

An attached point doesn't hold a position. It says "a quarter of the way along layer L3's path", or "on the tip of lobe 2 of layer L5". The other layer decides where it is, and the handle follows (Figure 24). It works one way only: dragging the attached handle slides it along the path; it never pulls the other layer out of shape. Anchored discs, a handle dropped mid-arm, and anything placed on scaffold all work like this.

[[FIG weld_attach | Point 14 lies on layer L3's path]]

Because attachments run one way, the layers can always be worked out in order: each one after the layers it is attached to (Figure 25). If you try to attach L6 to L5 when L5 is already attached to L6, there is no order that works, so Sketchpad refuses at that moment, with a message.

[[FIG eval_order | Layers are worked out in order; a loop is refused]]

Lesson 10. Putting it together: a figure with no code

Many of the pattern scripts are a figure written out as code. OverlappingStars.js works out twenty named points on a grid, then stitches parabolas between groups of them. In Version 2 that kind of drawing can be put together from layers instead (Figure 26). Layer G makes a 3-by-3 grid of named points and is marked as scaffold, so it never prints. Four Parabola layers each name three of G's points: two arm ends and the shared centre p5. The result is a four-pointed star.

[[FIG composed_star | A star composed from a grid, with no code]]

What to notice. Change the spacing of grid G and the star redraws at the new size, because its layers name G's points instead of copying them. Add a second grid offset by half a cell, with four more layers, and you have overlapping stars: the same idea as the script, but you can now drag it, weld it and print it.

Lesson 11. Writing your own generator

When composition isn't enough, you write a generator: one file, saved into generators/. It appears in the Insert list straight away. Listing 1 is a complete one that doesn't exist today: a spiral with each point joined to the point a fixed number of steps further along.

 1 /* generators/spiralWeb.js -- a spiral, each point joined to the point "gap" steps on. */
 2 export const meta = { id: "spiralWeb", version: 1, title: "Spiral Web",
 3                      tags: ["stitch", "spiral"], notes: "Skip-connected spiral." };
 4
 5 export const params = {
 6   centre: { type: "point", handle: true, default: [400, 400] },
 7   turns:  { type: "number", default: 4,  min: 1, max: 10, step: 0.5, label: "Turns" },
 8   steps:  { type: "int",    default: 80, min: 20, max: 300, label: "Points" },
 9   gap:    { type: "int",    default: 9,  min: 1, max: 60,  label: "Gap" },
10   size:   { type: "number", default: 120, min: 20, max: 380, label: "Size" },
11   color:  { type: "color",  default: "#0044cc" }
12 };
13
14 export function build(p, k) {
15   const spiral = k.spiral(p.centre, { turns: p.turns, outer: p.size }, p.steps);
16   return { paths: { spiral },
17            stitches: k.skip(spiral, p.gap, { wrap: false }),
18            points: { centre: p.centre, outerEnd: k.ends(spiral).end },
19            style: { color: p.color } };
20 }
Listing 1. A complete generator

Line by line:

  • Lines 2 to 3 name it. id is permanent, because saved figures refer to it.
  • Lines 5 to 12 declare the settings. Each says what kind of value it is, and the sliders are built from that. centre is a draggable point because it says handle: true.
  • Line 15 makes the path.
  • Line 17 connects it. The spiral is open, so wrap: false stops the skip from running past the end.
  • Line 18 names two points that other layers may attach to.

There is no init, update or draw, and nothing is stored between calls. Figure 27 shows the output with two values of Gap.

[[FIG spiral_web | Spiral Web, as Listing 1 draws it]]

Lesson 12. How today's objects come out

Each of the 14 Draw objects becomes a short recipe. The ones marked draft are first guesses, to be settled when each object's one-page feature list is written with you (specification 10.2).

ObjectRecipe
Lineline(a, b); the middle handle moves both ends
Parabolatwo line arms, pairwise; the corner is two handles until you weld them
Regular Polygonpolygon; pairwise at each corner between neighbouring sides
Mystic Rose, Mystic Rose (Ellipse)circle or ellipse, allPairs
Cycloidcircle (or ellipse), multiply(k)
Chords in Ellipseellipse, skip(s); draft: how its five modes map, from its feature list
Circular Paraboladraft: the Parabola recipe, repeated by rotation around a centre
Circular Parabola (Multi)as above; its second handle separates and joins the copies through the generator's own drag rule
Linked Circlesseveral circle paths, joined pairwise as pairs, a ring, or all to all
Parametricsparametric, evenSpacing, then any connector; what can be dragged is still to decide
Inverse Star, Radiate, Regular Pursuitdraft: from their feature lists

Lesson 13. What the model does not cover

The model is about points and lines, because nails and thread are. Fills, gradients, transparency and pixel effects don't fit it, and don't need to. Playpen scripts that work that way keep their own canvas inside the script host and paint directly, as they do today. They can still be shown, given thumbnails, and placed in a figure as a picture. They just can't give nails.

Quick reference: the kernel's vocabulary

FamilyNameMeaning
Makersline(a, b, n)n steps from a to b
circle(c, r, n), ellipse(c, w, h, n)n points round, closed
polygon(c, r, sides, n)sides with n steps each, closed
arc(c, r, from, to, n)part of a circle, open
spiral(c, options, n)a spiral, open
parametric(f, t0, t1, n)any rule p(t), sampled
ShapersevenSpacing(path, n)equal distances along the path
bias(path, b)crowd towards one end
jitter(path, size, seed)repeatable random nudges
trim(path, a, b)drop points from the ends
reverse(path)run backwards
startAt(path, i)renumber a closed path
everyKth(path, k)keep every k-th point
move, rotate, scale, mirror, split, joinplacement and assembly
Connectorspairwise(p, q)point i of p to point i of q
skip(path, s)point i to point i + s
multiply(path, k)point i to point k × i
allPairs(path)every point to every other
ring(paths, rule)each path to the next, round
between(paths, rule)several paths, pairs or all to all
Findersends, middlestart, end, halfway
extremestop, bottom, left, right
tips, cusps, centrefeatures of curves
crossings(p, q)where two paths cross

Closed paths wrap round: counting past the last point starts again at 0. When two paths of different lengths are connected, the connector either respaces one to match, or stops with a message that names both lengths and the missing point.
